new_statements.quote: Esto no ocurre en el idioma Akateko, donde el acento no es un valor distintivo semánticamente, es decir, no cambia el significado de la palabra, al igual que en el resto de los idiomas mayas. El acento en el idioma Akateko se puede decir que es agudo, porque la mayoría de las palabras lleva el acento en la última sílaba. [...] 2.3.3.2 El acento en los distintos tipos de palabras según su número de sílabas. Se reglamenta que en el idioma Maya Akateko todas las palabras que tengan dos sílabas en adelante son acentuadas en la última sílaba. Ejemplos: [...] Ante' an – te' 'fruta'; Mame ma – me 'papá' [...] K'anani k'a – na – ni 'apretado' [...] Mulnawom mul – na – wom 'trabajador'; B'aloneb' b'a – lo – neb' 'nueve'
new_statements.translation: This does not happen in Akateko, where stress has no semantically distinctive value, i.e. it does not change the meaning of the word, as in the rest of the Mayan languages. Stress in Akateko can be said to be 'agudo' (oxytone), because most words carry the stress on the last syllable. [...] 2.3.3.2 Stress in the different word types by number of syllables. It is ruled that in the Mayan language Akateko all words of two or more syllables are stressed on the last syllable. Examples: an-TE' 'fruit', ma-ME 'father', k'a-na-NI 'tight', mul-na-WOM 'worker', b'a-lo-NEB' 'nine' (stressed syllable underlined in the original).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable and non-contrastive; it falls on the final syllable of any polysyllabic word (disyllables, trisyllables and polysyllables all illustrated with the last syllable underlined).
new_statements.exceptions: None listed; the hedge 'la mayoría de las palabras' in 2.3.3.1 is followed by the categorical rule in 2.3.3.2. Monosyllables are said not to bear (locatable) stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the orthographic/citation word (isolated words, i.e. phrase-final forms). The book does not discuss phrase-medial vs phrase-final position; Bennett 2016 (citing England 2001) reports second-hand that Akatek, like Q'anjob'al, shows phrasal conditioning (initial stress phrase-medially, final stress phrase-finally), so the final-stress rule may strictly hold for phrase-final/citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: The ALMG normative grammar describes standard Akateko of the Comunidad Lingüística Akateka (San Miguel Acatán and San Rafael La Independencia, Huehuetenango) = Glottolog west2635 'Western Kanjobal/Akateko', ISO knj. Zavala's 1992 ALIM volume documents the same language as spoken by refugees on the Chiapas border ('Acateco de la frontera sur'); older literature calls it 'kanjobal de San Miguel Acatán', and some OKMA work treats it as a dialect of Q'anjob'al (kanj1263/qanj..), but all sources examined refer to the San Miguel Acatán variety.
